practicals.title: Cold booting, warm booting and shutting down a computer
practicals.aim: To boot a desktop computer from cold, restart it (warm boot), identify the main features of the Windows desktop and shut it down correctly.
apparatus: Desktop computer (system unit, monitor, keyboard, mouse)
Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) or surge protector
safety: Keep food and drinks out of the computer laboratory; a spilt drink can short-circuit a keyboard or system unit.
Do not touch power sockets, cables or the back of the system unit with wet hands; report frayed cables to the teacher.
Sit upright with the monitor at about arm's length and the top of the screen at eye level; rest your eyes every 20 minutes.
Never switch off at the wall socket or UPS while Windows is still running; it can corrupt files.
procedure: Check that the UPS is connected to the mains and the system unit and monitor are plugged into the UPS.
Switch on the UPS, then the monitor, then press the power button on the system unit. Start the timer.
Observe the power-on self-test (POST): the fans start, the manufacturer's logo appears and a single short beep is heard on most machines.
Watch the operating system load. Stop the timer when the desktop is ready and the pointer stops showing a busy circle. Record this cold-boot time.
Identify and write down the desktop features: icons (This PC, Recycle Bin), Start button, taskbar, notification area with the clock, and wallpaper.
Warm boot: click Start > Power > Restart (or press Ctrl + Alt + Delete and choose Restart). Time how long it takes to return to the desktop.
Save and close any open files, then click Start > Power > Shut down. Wait until the power light goes off before switching off the monitor and UPS.
practicals.expectedObservations: During a cold boot the POST runs first (memory check, keyboard lights flash) before Windows loads. A warm boot skips the full power-off and is usually quicker. On shut-down the screen shows "Shutting down" and the system unit switches itself off.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: cold-boot time = 48 s; warm-boot time = 22 s. Time saved by a warm boot = 48 - 22 = 26 s. As a fraction of the cold-boot time: 26 / 48 x 100 = 54.2% quicker. Record results in a table: Boot type | Start method | Time (s).
precautions: Close all programs and save work before restarting or shutting down.
Wait about 10 seconds after shut-down before switching the computer on again.
Use the Start menu, not the power button, for a normal shut-down.
sourcesOfError: Reaction time when starting and stopping the timer.
Background updates can make one boot slower than another.
commonMistakes: Confusing cold booting (starting from power off) with warm booting (restarting a machine that is already on).
Holding the power button to switch off a working computer.
Listing hardware (keyboard, mouse) when asked for desktop features.
examTips: Write the shut-down steps in order with the exact menu names (Start > Power > Shut down); each correct step usually earns a mark.
Give Ctrl + Alt + Delete or the Restart option/reset button as the methods of a warm boot.
When asked for differences, set them out in a two-column table.

checkQuestions.q: Which of these is a warm boot?
options: Choosing Restart from the Start menu
Pressing the power button on a computer that is off
checkQuestions.explanation: A warm boot restarts a computer that is already running.

checkQuestions.q: The self-test the computer runs when first switched on is called
A cold boot took 50 s and a warm boot 20 s. How much time did the warm boot save?
Which is NOT a desktop feature?
checkQuestions.explanation: The keyboard is a hardware input device.

practicals.title: Using the keyboard and mouse; measuring typing speed
practicals.aim: To classify the keys on a keyboard, carry out the main mouse operations and measure typing speed in words per minute.
materials: A printed passage of about 300 words (e.g. a short paragraph on Nigerian independence)
safety: Keep food and drinks out of the computer laboratory; a spilt drink can short-circuit a keyboard or system unit.
Do not touch power sockets, cables or the back of the system unit with wet hands; report frayed cables to the teacher.
Sit upright with the monitor at about arm's length and the top of the screen at eye level; rest your eyes every 20 minutes.
procedure: Study the keyboard and list examples of each group: function keys (F1-F12), alphabetic keys, numeric keys (top row and numeric keypad), cursor/arrow keys, and special keys (Enter, Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Esc, Tab, Backspace, Delete).
Mouse practice: point to an icon, single-click to select it, double-click to open it, right-click to show the shortcut menu, and drag a file icon to a new place on the desktop.
Open Notepad. Start the stopwatch and type the passage for exactly 5 minutes without looking at the keyboard as much as possible.
Stop typing at 5 minutes. Use the word processor's word/character count to find how many characters you typed.
Compare your work with the original and count the uncorrected errors.
Calculate gross and net speed as shown below.
practicals.expectedObservations: Single-click selects (the icon is highlighted); double-click opens; right-click shows a context menu; drag-and-drop moves the item. Caps Lock and Num Lock lights turn on and off when the keys are pressed.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A standard "word" is 5 characters (including spaces). Worked example: 1 500 characters typed in 5 minutes with 6 uncorrected errors. Words typed = 1 500 / 5 = 300 words. Gross speed = 300 / 5 = 60 wpm. Net speed = gross - (errors / minutes) = 60 - 6/5 = 58.8 wpm.
precautions: Keep fingers on the home keys (ASDF and JKL;) and return to them after each stroke.
Use the correct timing; stop exactly at the time limit.
Hold the mouse lightly with the wrist straight.
sourcesOfError: Miscounting errors
Starting or stopping the stopwatch late
commonMistakes: Calling the numeric keypad "function keys".
Dividing characters by minutes and forgetting to divide by 5 to get words.
Using Backspace and Delete as if they were the same (Backspace deletes to the left, Delete to the right of the cursor).
examTips: Give two named examples for each key group.
For mouse operations, state both the action and its result (e.g. "double-click - opens a file or program").
Always show the formula before substituting numbers in speed calculations.

checkQuestions.q: F1 to F12 are called
checkQuestions.explanation: They perform program-defined functions, e.g. F1 for Help.

Which key deletes the character to the LEFT of the cursor?
checkQuestions.explanation: Delete removes the character to the right.

practicals.title: Creating, formatting, saving and printing a document
practicals.aim: To create a one-page notice in Microsoft Word, apply character and paragraph formatting, set page margins, save it in a named folder and print it.
apparatus: Computer with Microsoft Word (or LibreOffice Writer)
materials: Text of a notice, e.g. "Inter-House Sports: Friday 14 March, 10 a.m., school field"
safety: Keep food and drinks out of the computer laboratory; a spilt drink can short-circuit a keyboard or system unit.
Do not touch power sockets, cables or the back of the system unit with wet hands; report frayed cables to the teacher.
Sit upright with the monitor at about arm's length and the top of the screen at eye level; rest your eyes every 20 minutes.
procedure: Start Word: Start > Word (or double-click its icon) and choose Blank document.
Type the heading and body text. Do not press Enter at the end of each line; let word wrap work.
Select the heading; make it bold (Ctrl + B), 16-point size and centred (Ctrl + E). Make the body 12-point Times New Roman, justified (Ctrl + J), with 1.5 line spacing.
Layout > Margins > Custom Margins: set all four margins to 2.54 cm on A4 portrait.
Insert a bulleted list of the events and a page border; use Find and Replace to change "House" to "house" where needed; run Spelling & Grammar (F7).
File > Save As: browse to Documents, create a folder named SS3 and save the file as Sports_Notice.docx.
File > Print: choose the printer, 1 copy, then click Print. Close the document (Ctrl + W) and exit Word.
practicals.expectedObservations: The heading appears bold, larger and centred; justified text has straight left and right edges; the title bar shows the file name after saving; the printout matches the screen (WYSIWYG).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Text width on A4 = page width - left margin - right margin = 21.0 - 2.54 - 2.54 = 15.92 cm. Font size: 72 points = 1 inch = 2.54 cm, so 12 pt = 12/72 x 2.54 = 0.42 cm high. A 16-pt heading is 16/12 = 1.33 times the height of 12-pt body text.
precautions: Select text before applying formatting.
Save early and often (Ctrl + S) to avoid losing work during a power cut.
Use Print Preview before printing to avoid wasting paper.
sourcesOfError: Printer scaling ("fit to page") changing the printed sizes
Different default fonts on different computers
commonMistakes: Pressing Enter at the end of every line instead of letting text wrap.
Using Save instead of Save As when asked to save with a new name.
Writing "click Bold" without first selecting the text.
examTips: Write steps using exact menu or ribbon names (Home > Font > Bold) or correct shortcuts; vague steps lose marks.
Know the shortcuts: Ctrl + C copy, Ctrl + V paste, Ctrl + X cut, Ctrl + Z undo, Ctrl + S save, Ctrl + A select all, Ctrl + P print.
Hand in the printout with your name and index number in the header or footer if instructed.

checkQuestions.explanation: Ctrl + E centres; Ctrl + J justifies; Ctrl + L aligns left.

options: save a file with a new name or location
checkQuestions.explanation: Save overwrites the existing file; Save As creates a new copy.

checkQuestions.explanation: Word wrap avoids pressing Enter at the end of every line.

practicals.title: Mail merge: personalised letters to parents
practicals.aim: To produce personalised letters to many parents by merging a main letter with a data source.
apparatus: Computer with Microsoft Word and Excel
materials: Excel list of parents (Title, Surname, StudentName, Class)
Draft letter inviting parents to the PTA meeting
safety: Keep food and drinks out of the computer laboratory; a spilt drink can short-circuit a keyboard or system unit.

procedure: Prepare the data source in Excel with headings in row 1: Title, Surname, StudentName, Class. Enter the records and save as Parents.xlsx.
In Word, type the main letter, leaving blanks for the personal details.
Mailings > Start Mail Merge > Letters. Then Select Recipients > Use an Existing List and choose Parents.xlsx.
Place the cursor where each detail goes and use Insert Merge Field to insert <<Title>> <<Surname>>, <<StudentName>> and <<Class>>.
Click Preview Results and use the arrows to check several letters.

practicals.expectedObservations: In preview each letter shows a different parent's name and child; the merged document contains one letter per record.

Preview before merging to catch spacing mistakes such as "Mr.Okeke".

Blank rows produce empty letters

Forgetting to name the two files combined: the main document and the data source.
examTips: State clearly that mail merge combines a main document (form letter) with a data source (list of names and addresses).
Number the steps and use the Mailings tab names.

checkQuestions.explanation: The data source holds the names and addresses.

checkQuestions.q: Which tab in Word holds the mail merge tools?
checkQuestions.explanation: Mailings contains Start Mail Merge, Insert Merge Field and Finish & Merge.

practicals.title: Spreadsheet result sheet with SUM, AVERAGE, MAX and IF
practicals.aim: To build a class result sheet in Excel using formulae and built-in functions, copy formulae with the fill handle and add a remark using IF.
apparatus: Computer with Microsoft Excel (or LibreOffice Calc)
materials: Scores of five students in three subjects
safety: Keep food and drinks out of the computer laboratory; a spilt drink can short-circuit a keyboard or system unit.
Do not touch power sockets, cables or the back of the system unit with wet hands; report frayed cables to the teacher.
Sit upright with the monitor at about arm's length and the top of the screen at eye level; rest your eyes every 20 minutes.
procedure: In row 1 type the headings: A1 Name, B1 Maths, C1 English, D1 Biology, E1 Total, F1 Average, G1 Remark.
Enter the data in A2:D6: Ngozi 72, 65, 80; Tunde 55, 48, 61; Hauwa 38, 52, 45; Emeka 90, 84, 77; Zainab 61, 59, 70.
In E2 type =SUM(B2:D2) and press Enter. In F2 type =AVERAGE(B2:D2). In G2 type =IF(F2>=50,"PASS","FAIL").
Select E2:G2 and drag the fill handle down to row 6.
In B7 type =MAX(B2:B6) and in B8 type =AVERAGE(B2:B6). Label A7 "Highest" and A8 "Mean".
Format F2:F6 to 2 decimal places; make row 1 bold; add borders; save as Results.xlsx and print with gridlines.
practicals.expectedObservations: When the formula is copied down, the cell references change (B2:D2 becomes B3:D3 and so on); results update automatically if a score is changed. The formula appears in the formula bar while the value appears in the cell.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Totals: Ngozi 217, Tunde 164, Hauwa 135, Emeka 251, Zainab 190. Averages (2 d.p.): 72.33, 54.67, 45.00, 83.67, 63.33. Remarks: PASS, PASS, FAIL, PASS, PASS. Highest Maths =MAX(B2:B6) = 90; mean Maths =AVERAGE(B2:B6) = 316/5 = 63.2.
precautions: Begin every formula with an equals sign (=).
Use cell references, not typed numbers, so results update automatically.
Put text inside IF in double quotation marks.
sourcesOfError: Typing a score into the wrong cell
Rounding displayed values versus stored values
commonMistakes: Writing =B2+C2+D2/3 for the average (only D2 is divided by 3).
Leaving out the quotation marks around "PASS".
Writing SUM(B2:D2) without the = sign, so Excel shows it as text.
examTips: Write formulas exactly as they would be typed, e.g. =AVERAGE(B2:D2), and state the value produced.
When asked what appears after copying, give both the new formula and the values.
Show the arithmetic for each value; marks are given for both formula and result.

checkQuestions.explanation: Relative references change by the number of rows moved.

checkQuestions.explanation: 49.5 is not greater than or equal to 50.

practicals.title: Relative and absolute cell references: VAT calculation
practicals.aim: To use an absolute reference ($B$1) to calculate 7.5% VAT on a list of prices and compare the result with a relative reference.
materials: Price list of four items in naira
safety: Keep food and drinks out of the computer laboratory; a spilt drink can short-circuit a keyboard or system unit.
Do not touch power sockets, cables or the back of the system unit with wet hands; report frayed cables to the teacher.
Sit upright with the monitor at about arm's length and the top of the screen at eye level; rest your eyes every 20 minutes.
procedure: In A1 type VAT Rate and in B1 type 7.5%.
In A3:A6 enter the prices 2000, 3500, 1200 and 8000. Type headings Price, VAT and Total in row 2.
In B3 type =A3*$B$1 and copy it down to B6. Click B5 and read the formula in the formula bar.
In C3 type =A3+B3 and copy down to C6. In C7 type =SUM(C3:C6).
In D3 type =A3*B1 (no dollar signs) and copy it down to D6. Note what happens.
Format B3:C7 as Currency (N) with 2 decimal places and save as VAT.xlsx.
practicals.expectedObservations: The formula in B5 is =A5*$B$1: A changes but $B$1 stays fixed. In the relative version the rate reference moves too: D4 becomes =A4*B2 (an empty cell, so 0) and D5, D6 multiply by VAT values instead of the rate, giving wrong answers.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: VAT = price x 7.5%: 2000 -> 150.00; 3500 -> 262.50; 1200 -> 90.00; 8000 -> 600.00. Totals: 2150.00, 3762.50, 1290.00, 8600.00. =SUM(C3:C6) = 15 802.50. With =A3*B1 copied down: D3 = 150 is correct, but D4 = A4*B2 = 3500 x 0 = 0 (B2 is empty), D5 = A5*B3 = 1200 x 150 = 180 000 and D6 = A6*B4 = 8000 x 262.5 = 2 100 000, which are nonsense values. This shows why an absolute reference is needed.
precautions: Press F4 after typing a cell reference to add the $ signs.
Enter percentages with the % sign or as a decimal (0.075).
sourcesOfError: Typing 7.5 instead of 7.5% gives VAT 100 times too big
commonMistakes: Leaving out the $ signs, so the rate cell reference moves when copied.
Placing $ only before the column ($B1), which still lets the row change when copied down.
examTips: Explain the difference in one sentence: a relative reference changes when copied; an absolute reference ($B$1) does not.
When asked for the formula in another cell after copying, adjust only the relative parts.

checkQuestions.q: =A3*$B$1 in B3 is copied to B6. The formula in B6 is
checkQuestions.explanation: Only the relative reference A3 changes.

checkQuestions.explanation: F4 cycles through absolute and mixed references.

practicals.title: Making a straight-through network cable (RJ45, T568B)
practicals.aim: To identify common computer and network cables and connectors, and to crimp and test a straight-through Cat 6 patch cable.
apparatus: Sample cables: USB, HDMI/VGA, power, coaxial, telephone (RJ11)
safety: Handle the stripper and crimper blades carefully; cut away from your body.
Collect off-cuts of copper wire; they can cause short circuits if they fall into equipment.
Do not test cables connected to mains equipment.
procedure: Identify and label the sample cables and their connectors (male/female): USB, VGA/HDMI, power (IEC), coaxial with T-connector/BNC, telephone RJ11, network RJ45.
Measure and cut the UTP cable to length; slide on the boots.
Strip about 2.5 cm of the outer jacket without nicking the inner wires; untwist the pairs.
Arrange the wires in T568B order: white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown. Trim them straight to about 1.3 cm.
Push the wires fully into the RJ45 plug (clip facing down) so each reaches the end; crimp firmly. Repeat at the other end in the same order.
Test with the cable tester: lights 1 to 8 should light in the same order on both units.
practicals.expectedObservations: A good cable shows lights 1-8 in sequence on both ends. A missing light shows an open wire; lights out of order show a crossed pair.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Lab of 12 computers, each about 6 m from the switch plus 0.5 m slack: cable = 12 x 6.5 = 78 m. Connectors: 2 per cable = 24; adding 10% for mistakes, 24 x 1.1 = 26.4, so buy 27. A 305 m box of cable leaves 305 - 78 = 227 m.
precautions: Keep the untwisted length short to reduce interference.
Check the colour order twice before crimping.
sourcesOfError: Wires not pushed fully into the plug
Damaged insulation when stripping
commonMistakes: Using T568A at one end and T568B at the other (that makes a crossover cable).
Crimping with the outer jacket outside the plug, so the strain relief fails.
examTips: Name each cable with its connector: twisted pair - RJ45; telephone - RJ11; coaxial - BNC/T-connector; fibre optic - ST/SC.
Recite the T568B colour order.

practicals.title: Drawing and comparing network topologies
practicals.aim: To identify the network devices in the school laboratory and draw star, bus and ring topologies, comparing their cabling needs.
safety: Do not unplug network devices without permission.
procedure: Tour the laboratory and identify the switch/hub, router, modem and network interface cards (NIC) on the computers.
Draw the laboratory as a star topology with 12 computers connected to a central switch.
Draw a bus topology with the same computers on a single backbone with terminators at both ends.
Draw a ring topology with each computer joined to two neighbours.
Count the cables or links needed for each and list one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
practicals.expectedObservations: The laboratory uses a star layout: every cable runs from a computer to the switch, so one faulty cable affects only one computer.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Star with 12 PCs: 12 cables; a 16-port switch leaves 16 - 12 = 4 free ports. Ring with 12 PCs: 12 links. Bus: 1 backbone, 12 drop connections and 2 terminators.
precautions: Label each device in drawings.
sourcesOfError: Hidden cabling in trunking may be miscounted
commonMistakes: Drawing a hub/switch in a bus topology.
Confusing a LAN (one building) with a WAN (wide area).
examTips: Draw neat, labelled diagrams; each correct diagram usually earns separate marks.
Give the function of each device: switch, router, modem, NIC, bridge.

checkQuestions.q: In which topology does every computer connect to a central device?
checkQuestions.explanation: A star uses a hub or switch.

practicals.title: Running an antivirus scan and securing a computer
practicals.aim: To update antivirus software, scan a flash drive and the hard disk, deal with detected threats and check the firewall.
apparatus: Computer with antivirus software (e.g. Microsoft Defender, Avast)
safety: Keep food and drinks out of the computer laboratory; a spilt drink can short-circuit a keyboard or system unit.
Do not touch power sockets, cables or the back of the system unit with wet hands; report frayed cables to the teacher.
Sit upright with the monitor at about arm's length and the top of the screen at eye level; rest your eyes every 20 minutes.
Never deliberately open a suspected virus file.
procedure: Open the antivirus program and update its virus definitions.
Insert the flash drive; right-click it in This PC and choose Scan with the antivirus before opening any files.
Run a Quick scan of the computer, then start a Full scan; note the number of files scanned, threats found and time taken.
Quarantine or delete any threats as advised by the program.
Open Windows Security > Firewall & network protection and confirm that the firewall is on.
Record the result and list three habits that prevent infection.
practicals.expectedObservations: The program shows progress, files scanned and threats found; a quarantined file is moved to a safe area where it cannot run.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Scan time worked example: 120 GB of data scanned at 40 MB/s takes 120 x 1 024 / 40 = 3 072 s = 51.2 minutes. Scanning only the 8 GB flash drive at the same rate: 8 x 1 024 / 40 = 204.8 s, about 3.4 minutes.
precautions: Update definitions before scanning.
Do not interrupt a full scan.
sourcesOfError: Scan speed varies with file types and disk speed
commonMistakes: Opening files on a flash drive before scanning it.
Confusing a firewall with antivirus software.
examTips: Name examples of antivirus software (Norton, McAfee, Avast) and preventive measures such as firewalls, encryption and care with attachments.
Distinguish viruses, worms and Trojan horses.
